Broiled
broyld
v. (past participle of broil; cooked by direct exposure to fire)
Old French bruler, to burn — to cook meat or fish by direct exposure to flame or coals.

Biblical Definition

And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.

Broiled fish is the single, deliberately unspectacular detail Luke records at the moment the risen Christ proves his body is not a vision. He has just shown his hands and his feet and invited them to handle him and see; and then, still met with disbelief for joy, he asks for something to eat, and they hand him ordinary broiled fish and honeycomb. No detail in the Gospels does more quiet work against every impulse to make the resurrection a merely spiritual or symbolic event. A ghost does not eat broiled fish. Luke chose the plainest possible food, prepared the plainest possible way, because the plainness itself is the argument: this is a real body, in a real room, eating a real supper.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from BROIL: to cook or dress by direct exposure to fire, on a gridiron or coals, without the intervention of water.

expand to see more

BROIL, v.t. To cook by direct exposure to fire, on a gridiron or coals.

To subject to great heat.

BROILED, pp. Cooked by direct exposure to fire; dressed on a gridiron.

A plain, common method of preparing fish or flesh, requiring no elaborate process.

Used in Luke's Gospel of the fish given to the risen Christ, proof of his bodily reality.

Key Scripture

Luk 24:42 — "And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb."

Modern Corruption

A gnostic instinct, ancient and still current, prefers a resurrection that is spiritual, symbolic, or merely inspirational, and finds a detail as plain as broiled fish an embarrassment to be spiritualized away rather than the deliberate proof Luke intended it to be.

expand to see more

Every age has produced a version of the same doubt the disciples first felt: surely something this important cannot really be about a body eating fish. Luke's answer is to record exactly that, without apology, because the plainness is the whole force of the proof.

A faith that quietly prefers a spiritualized resurrection to a bodily one has more in common with the disciples' initial disbelief for joy than with the apostolic testimony that followed it. Broiled fish and honeycomb are unglamorous on purpose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

No Hebrew or Greek headword of doctrinal weight; the significance is entirely in the plainness of the detail Luke chooses to record.

expand to see more

Broiled fish follows immediately after Christ's invitation to handle his hands and feet.

The detail answers the disciples' disbelief for joy with the plainest possible proof.

A ghost, by definition, does not eat broiled fish.

Honeycomb alongside it makes the meal ordinary, not ceremonial.

Luke's Gospel builds its resurrection case on plain, checkable details like this one.

Usage

"A piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb — the plainest possible meal, deliberately recorded."

"Given immediately after Christ's invitation to handle him and see."

"The detail argues against every spiritualized reading of the resurrection body."
